newsitem.title: USA: Rangebound dlr little changed to weaker at US noon.
newsitem.headline: Rangebound dlr little changed to weaker at US noon.

text.p: The dollar was little changed versus the yen at midday as traders weighed the risk of Bank of Japan (BOJ) intervention despite the mild statement from Group of Seven (G7) officials this weekend, experts said.
The greenback remained slightly weaker against the mark at midday, pressured by selling of sterling for marks, they said.
"Everbody is thinking about intervention from Japan," said a trader at the New York branch of a Japanese bank.
But the trader also said he believed the dollar would eventually go higher if the BOJ intervened without the Federal Reserve or European central banks.
Specifically, the trader said market players are concerned about the possibility of the BOJ selling dollars for yen when the dollar climbs above 127 yen.
The dollar stood at 126.65/75 yen at midday, up slightly from 126.63/73 at the open but well below the overnight high of 127.10. The dollar fell to 1.7280/90 marks from 1.7316/19.
Traders cited selling of dollar/yen by funds but also noted talk of a Japanese buyer near 126.50 yen.
The G7 statement said exchange rates should reflect economic fundamentals and deemed excessive volatility undesirable.
The G7 statement also emphasized the importance of avoiding exchange rates that could lead to the reemergence of large external imbalances.

"The point is, the U.S. Administration is concerned about the trade deficit (with Japan) but not to the extent that they would join the Japanese in intervening against the dollar," said Brian McCarthy, a market analyst at Ruesch International.

Prior to midday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin told an International Monetary Fund committee that he saw a risk of rising trade surpluses in some industrial nations and called on those nations to promote domestic demand and open markets.
Although Rubin did not mention any specific countries, he and other U.S. officials have warned Japan to avoid a significant rise in its current account surplus.
"Rubin's comments, I think, have to be interpreted as at least putting a cap on dollar/yen," said Paul Park, a vice president of foreign exchange at Mellon Bank N.A.
Still Park said dollar/yen may grind higher because the "carry trade" is still very profitable.
The dollar slipped below 1.73 marks early in the session, and traders attributed this, in part, to sterling/mark sales.
There seems to be some profit-taking on long sterling positions in the approach to the election on Thursday, said Steven Walker, a senior trader at Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken in New York.
The U.K. election will be held on May 1.
In early afternoon activity, sterling traded near 2.8070/80 marks, down from around 2.8120/30 marks in early dealings.
The currency markets face a barrage of potentially market moving data later this week, including crucial U.S. employment figures for April that are due out on Friday.
A lot depends on what we see this week with the U.S. figures, McCarthy said. Forecasts point to the kind of data that will sustain speculation for a U.S. interest rate hike.
U.S. non-farm payrolls are expected to show a 211,000 gain in April after adding 175,000 in March, based on the consensus forecast from a Reuters poll.
In other trade, the dollar fell to 1.4684/94 Swiss francs from 1.4725/35, but rose to Canadian $1.3991/96 from C$1.3978/83. The pound slid to $1.6230/40 from $1.6235/45.
